title: Making the Most of One-on-One Meetings With Team Members
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article contrasts two models of the weekly one-on-one meeting: the common approach where leaders set the agenda and drive feedback, versus a markedly different approach used by top leaders and coaches, who hand ownership of the conversation to the team member. Rather than directing the discussion, these leaders treat themselves as a resource and ask questions like what the team member wants to explore or what obstacles are in their way. Any direction the leader wants to offer is saved for the end of the meeting, after the team member feels heard. The author notes this can feel foreign at first in organizations unused to it, but argues that once team members recognize the meeting is truly theirs, leaders often find that much of the feedback they planned to deliver has already surfaced organically.
points: Most leaders default to setting the agenda and driving feedback in one-on-ones.
The best leaders and coaches flip the script, letting the team member own and direct the conversation.
Leaders reframe their role as a resource, asking what the team member needs rather than dictating direction.
Any coaching or direction the leader wants to add is saved until the end of the meeting.
Once team members feel heard, they become far more receptive to feedback from the leader.
quotes: One-on-one meetings are an invaluable opportunity for leaders to build relationships, provide guidance, and work through problems with their team members.
Study the best leaders and coaches, however, and you will see a markedly different approach to these weekly discussions.
They promote the idea that this is the team member’s opportunity to discuss and explore what they need to, not the other way around.
If these leaders perceive a need to offer direction or to make a point, they save this for the conclusion of the meeting.
Great leaders pull from others more than they push their agendas.
When team members learn the weekly one-on-ones are about their needs and issues, leaders learn much of the feedback they thought they needed to push has already been internalized.
